bad_beats: The supplied SOURCE doesn't establish that the free period ended, so it can't support the requested chapter without additional evidence. It says Square Enix suspended subscription fees after the backlash. It doesn't say those fees resumed, when players became liable for payment or what continued access required. Removing the rejected date alone wouldn't resolve that gap. Describing players paying while the replacement was unfinished would still assert an event absent from the permitted text. This is the central event of the proposed chapter, so implying it would preserve the problem identified in the rejection.

The replacement announcement presents a separate sourcing gap. The supplied Overview confirms that Yoshida ultimately replaced the original game, but it doesn't date an announcement. Development discusses the original game's creation and problems. It doesn't provide the later update calendar, the transfer of replacement features or the testing process described in the rejected draft. Those details must stay out of a rewrite restricted to this excerpt. The two links in the brief are separate references. Using their contents would expand the evidence beyond the SOURCE text your instructions currently permit, even though the brief points toward them.

The remaining supported material also overlaps heavily with the chapters already completed. Fee suspension, Yoshida's appointment, limited improvements and the replacement decision have already been covered. Retelling them at chapter length would violate your instruction to avoid repetition. The unused development details concern the original game's art and world construction. They don't establish the billing decision or its reception. A chapter built around those details would change the subject. Adding general observations about trust or subscription value would produce commentary, but it wouldn't supply the missing historical sequence that this chapter needs.

Please add the relevant announcement and billing passages to SOURCE, or explicitly allow the two linked references as evidence. The needed material must establish the announcement date, the resumption of billing and the replacement's status when charging began. Any payment conditions or discounts also need direct support if they're included. With that boundary resolved, the chapter can connect the running original to the payment decision and then look toward its approaching shutdown. Until then, these paragraphs are a source clarification, not documentary narration. They shouldn't be used as the chapter's spoken script.

November 11, 2012, is the server closure date established by the supplied SOURCE. The excerpt stops short of describing the ending. It doesn't name End of an Era. Bahamut isn't mentioned either. Neither detail appears anywhere in the supplied excerpt. That gap matters under your source rule. The opening scene needs a passage connecting the shutdown with the cinematic and its events. Otherwise, the chapter would present an unsupported sequence as documented history. These paragraphs flag the missing evidence. They aren't a finished documentary chapter. They shouldn't be recorded or published as narration. The requested scene remains unsupported here.

The Overview describes a Garlean Legatus's plot to bring a moon down on Eorzea. That establishes the threat. It doesn't establish the outcome. The excerpt supplies no account of the cinematic's events or their relationship to the shutdown. The setup can't prove the resolution. Filling those gaps from familiarity with Final Fantasy 14 would break the instruction to use only this SOURCE. A supporting passage needs to identify what happens and connect it to the service ending. Without that passage, the central scene would depend on outside knowledge. The existing plot summary doesn't provide the missing evidence.

The Overview also describes Yoshida's decision to replace the original game. It doesn't attribute the shutdown's storytelling treatment. Those are separate decisions. His documented leadership doesn't establish who conceived the cinematic or chose its connection to the replacement. That attribution needs its own evidence. Naming him as the author of this specific choice would exceed the supplied account. The chapter therefore needs a passage identifying the relevant decision and anyone responsible for it. Otherwise, individual credit should remain unassigned. The missing support concerns both the events shown and the creative choices that made the shutdown part of the narrative.

The earlier question must remain unanswered here. The supplied text doesn't explain how a server shutdown became part of the story. A replacement alone doesn't establish that connection. The necessary passage must connect the original ending to the replacement's fictional history. Please provide the omitted shutdown and story transition material, including the cinematic description. That would support the requested scene. It would also permit a direct answer to the earlier question and an ending grounded in evidence. Adding more narrative now would repeat earlier chapters or introduce unsupported events. This excerpt cannot substantiate the chapter's central claim.

good_beats: In 2009, Square Enix announced Final Fantasy 14. Its pedigree wouldn't excuse an unfinished game. The announced versions were for PC and PlayStation 3. This was the series' 2nd massively multiplayer online role-playing game, after Final Fantasy 11. Square Enix had decided these games belonged in the main numbered series. The developers still had doubts. They worried the finished game might be too radical for that name.

Planning had begun in 2005 under the codename Rapture. Producer Hiromichi Tanaka had held the same job on the earlier online game. His credits also included several early entries in the series. Director Nobuaki Komoto had directed the earlier online game. Writer Yaeko Sato had been its main scenario writer. The continuity was substantial. But Sato arrived after the new setting and gameplay had been decided. To use major locations in particular ways, she needed to consult her colleagues. Her story had to fit their world.

What did they want you to find there? Art director Akihiko Yoshida was moving from a static project to one built for updates and expansion. His earlier work included Vagrant Story and Final Fantasy 12. The team began with a detailed profile of Hydaelyn. It covered climate, geography and ecosystems. Those details were meant to make the fantasy feel real. Travel was supposed to be seamless. Eorzea's five playable races drew on the earlier game's original five. Their designs changed for the new setting. Familiarity mattered, even as the team tried to build something distinct.

That care reached down to individual expressions. A character artist adjusted faces by hand, while motion capture supplied the basis for movement. The team then sharpened those movements. In Limsa Lominsa's opening scene, a giant sea serpent's fins were animated individually. Even the monsters had carefully placed hair follicles. Underneath it all was Crystal Tools, the engine also used for Final Fantasy 13. The team adapted it for this game. It proved unsuitable, leaving the game's internal structure broken.

How much was that detail costing the world around it? A later development postmortem blamed an unhealthy focus on graphics over gameplay content. Its example was a flowerpot. It had as many polygons and lines of shader code as a player character. The graphical demands limited the screen to twenty players at once. You could admire the detail. But that limit undercut the communal appeal of a massively multiplayer game. Seamless travel carried another compromise. To save memory, the team repeatedly reused environmental features and textures. You were meant to explore, but the scenery had to repeat.

The console plans had complications of their own. Attempts to bring the game to Xbox 360 fell through over disagreements with Microsoft about Xbox Live. The PC release was approaching. Square Enix had put another online world inside its main series. Experienced developers had filled it with carefully crafted details. Those names couldn't tell you whether it was finished. Would that promised PlayStation version ever reach players? On September 30, 2010, the PC audience would get its turn to judge the result.

In 2010, Final Fantasy 14 put you in Eorzea as the Garlean Empire invaded. Its graphics impressed reviewers; playing it left a much worse impression. The music also earned praise. But the gameplay and interface drew condemnation, along with the sense that the game wasn't finished. If you were choosing an online world, those criticisms reached the things you'd use throughout your time there. A beautiful setting could get your attention. It couldn't settle whether you wanted to stay.

You could see how much work had gone into the presentation. Square Enix's in-house CGI company, Visual Works, made the opening cinematic. Character production was elaborate too. The team first sculpted models at high resolution, then reduced their polygon counts while keeping equivalent graphical quality. One technique let different-looking equipment share the same model data. Separate equipment tools could change shapes or alter the color and texture of materials. Those were specific solutions to visual problems. They didn't answer the criticism of the gameplay or the interface. The launch made that gap public.

Why hadn't that production effort delivered a better launch? An alpha test and a delayed beta had preceded release. A later postmortem pointed to Square Enix's outdated development methods. Under Tanaka and Komoto, the team was still working with a mindset from the 6th console generation. The 7th required more staff and resources. The old approach couldn't keep up. For you, those production problems arrived as a game critics considered unfinished.

The team also lacked experience developing MMORPGs. Final Fantasy 11 had encountered the same difficulty, but its developers had overcome it. That comparison offered a reason to believe the problem could be solved. It didn't excuse the state of the game. You were judging the game you could actually use. And the backlash came from fans as well as critics. Square Enix had to respond.

Square Enix suspended subscription fees because of the backlash. How far would the response reach beyond PC players? The company also indefinitely postponed the PlayStation 3 version. If you were waiting for that release, the wait now had no fixed end. PC players had a game under criticism. Prospective console players had an indefinite delay. The launch had changed both the subscription plans and the console plans. Square Enix's response would also reach the people running the game.

The 2010 version of Final Fantasy 14 was still running when Square Enix replaced its development leadership. Producer and director Naoki Yoshida would now lead the response. An appointment couldn't repair a game. This was a handover inside a game that players could already enter and judge for themselves. Tanaka and Komoto had held the jobs separately. Yoshida now held both. He inherited the result of decisions made before his appointment, along with responsibility for what followed. Changing the leadership was concrete. Whether that change could improve the experience was a different question, and an appointment couldn't answer it.

Subscriptions stayed suspended while console players waited. Those measures framed the job Yoshida was taking on. For someone already playing, a different name in charge wasn't something you could test inside the game. You could only judge what the team delivered. The same distinction applied to the company. Replacing its leadership was an action Square Enix could take; making the game better required changes players could actually feel. Players still needed a better game. The handover established who would lead that work. Yoshida decided to make marginal improvements before the game's shutdown, with the original version still running during that work. But what did the game itself say about relying on others?

Yoshitaka Amano, the game's logo designer, had arranged adventurers in a wheel. Their backs were exposed. Weapons mattered to the design, but so did the need for comrades and friends. Support was part of the picture. That image offers a way to understand the handover without pretending a new leader had already rescued anything. Players depended on Square Enix to develop the game around them. The company had changed its leadership; the players still needed the result to be worth their time.

Yoshida had taken over a game that still existed, with its eventual fate unsettled by the appointment alone. The original servers would close on November 11, 2012. The server closure raises a question beyond who occupied the top jobs. How could a server shutdown become part of the story those players were following? Changing the leadership didn't answer it. What changed immediately was responsibility for the response. The launch still belonged to the team that made it. Square Enix had placed both production and direction in Yoshida's hands.

In 2010, Final Fantasy 14 put players inside Eorzea on technology that couldn't meet the game's needs. Square Enix couldn't save the original game with patches because its engine was unsuitable and its internal structure was broken. That made replacement a reasonable response. Yoshida could improve what players already had without treating that version as the game's permanent future. Those were different decisions. The repairs addressed the existing experience; a new version would address what came after it. Keeping the original going would therefore mean working on something that was ultimately going to be replaced.

The difficult distinction was between making the original better and making it the basis for everything that followed. Yoshida's limited repairs left room for the first. His decision to replace the game ruled out the second. For you, an improvement still mattered in the version available to play. A future replacement couldn't, by itself, improve the game already on your computer. Equally, a better experience in the original wouldn't establish that its underlying technology was suitable. The two efforts answered different needs. But the original still had a story to tell.

Sato's central narrative ran alongside side stories. The planned conflict put Eorzea's 5 main races against the beastmen, with the Garlean Empire as another force. Within that fiction, players faced the primals, the deities of the beastmen tribes. Eventually, a Garlean Legatus would plot to bring one of the planet's moons down on Eorzea. The world had dangers of its own. Those gave players something to follow beyond the condition of the software. An engine problem belonged to the people making the game; the threat of a falling moon belonged to its story. Choosing a replacement explained the technical response. It didn't, by itself, explain how the original world's story should end.

So what had the rebuild decision changed? Yoshida's response separated the original version's remaining life from the future of the game. Limited improvements could serve the former, while a replacement would carry the latter. The original could become better without becoming permanent. That was the boundary patches couldn't cross. You could judge an update by what it improved, but the replacement would have to establish its own worth. Choosing it settled the direction, not the result. The new version would carry the subtitle A Realm Reborn, and the original still had an ending ahead.

In August 2013, Final Fantasy 14 A Realm Reborn opened to players worldwide. Yoshida's rebuild earned its second chance by making the basics matter. The promised PlayStation version finally reached players on PS3, alongside the PC release. The wait was over. But reaching a console also meant designing for the person holding its controller. Yoshida made controller play a priority. He wanted experienced MMO players and Final Fantasy fans who'd never tried the genre to share the same game. Both groups had to feel welcome.

The engine underneath it was new. The server infrastructure had been improved too. Square Enix had demonstrated Luminous through its Agni's Philosophy tech demo. But Yoshida said Luminous and Crystal Tools were optimized for offline games. They couldn't handle an online environment with hundreds of character models. He called the replacement a "completely different engine." It shared structural similarities with Luminous, enough for Yoshida to call them siblings. Those similarities didn't make them interchangeable. The rebuild needed technology suited to the world its players would share.

How would Yoshida keep approvals from slowing the rebuild? He made about 400 fundamental design decisions to cut time spent waiting for approval. Standard genre features came first. The team had tested its new development workflow through updates to the original game. Those updates also provided a testing ground for features intended for the relaunch. The process carried into A Realm Reborn. Gameplay, the interface and the story were all revamped. Players with limited free time shaped the design too. That concern produced the Duty Finder system. The base game and its patch cycle also aimed to make returning easier for lapsed players. The invitation had to work for someone coming back after a break.

Existing PC players had been promised the new client free of charge. Character data and progress would transfer too. You could bring that history with you. The story made room for a return as well. Eorzea was now five years beyond the Seventh Umbral Calamity. Through temporal magic, the original player character had escaped and reappeared at the start of A Realm Reborn. The region was recovering, with another Garlean invasion to confront. The rebuild gave returning players a changed world and a way to carry their old characters into it.

But would the changes hold up once critics judged the game? The reception was largely positive. Critics praised the mechanics and progression, and credited Yoshida with an unexpected recovery. Solid mechanics sounded like a modest achievement. For this game, they were the point. Yoshida later described the workload at the Game Developers Conference. The team maintained one online game while building another over two years and eight months. The replacement had finally reached both PC and console players. Square Enix had given them a reason to try again. Now its rebuilt server infrastructure would have to serve the audience Yoshida had worked to reach.

In August 2013, Final Fantasy 14 A Realm Reborn was back in players' hands. Rebuilding the game had given Square Enix another chance, but keeping it meant earning players' trust beyond launch. This was a subscription game. If you kept paying, the experience had to keep justifying the bill. That made the recovery an ongoing obligation. Square Enix had also come through a poor 2013 fiscal year. The company had its own reason to care about what happened after launch.

The stakes extended beyond one title. On the original game's anniversary, Square Enix President Yoichi Wada said its launch had "greatly damaged" the Final Fantasy brand. That was the company's own assessment. Wada had already issued a formal apology to players and fans in December 2010. Now the replacement had to stand behind those words. A better game could begin that repair. Asking people to keep paying meant asking them to keep trusting the company that had apologized.

How could players judge what Square Enix was promising? Yoshida had addressed that during the recovery through his "Letters from the Producer". He discussed design direction, upcoming changes and player feedback. The aim was greater transparency. You could see what the team intended to do, then compare that with what it delivered. The distinction mattered. Announcing a change couldn't substitute for making it. Yoshida's priorities were to restore trust while improving playability. The letters gave players a way to follow those intentions before the next update arrived.

Yoshida's later diagnosis explained why promises needed scrutiny. He identified a belief that future patches could fix every problem as one cause of the original failure. He also criticized the pursuit of graphical quality at the expense of server performance. The original game had tens of thousands of high definition assets. He considered that approach unsustainable online. The trade-off was tangible. A subscription asked players to pay for the whole experience, including the parts no screenshot could show.

But what would all this work mean for Square Enix's finances? A subscription business depends on people continuing to pay. For you, that makes the promise personal every time another payment comes around. The company needed players who would stay. Its poor fiscal year gave that question weight beyond the game itself. Reaching release had settled one part of the rebuilding effort. The 2014 financial results would reveal whether the rebuilt game could help repair Square Enix's business.

In 2014, Square Enix credited Final Fantasy 14 A Realm Reborn with helping it return to profit. The relaunch became a commercial success. The company pointed to strong sales and the game's subscriber base. Square Enix attributed only part of its recovery to the game. That qualification matters. But a project that had needed replacing was now helping the company make money.

Yoshida's Legacy Campaign had given continuing players a specific reason to stay. During redevelopment, players who paid for at least three months qualified for permanently reduced monthly payments. An exclusive chocobo mount accompanied the discount. Qualifying players also got their names in the replacement's credits. The fees helped fund redevelopment. Square Enix, in turn, committed to charging those players less each month. If you'd stayed, that acknowledgment would follow you into your monthly bill. You were helping finance the recovery, with a lasting benefit attached.

How long could a recovery like that last? The years after relaunch began to answer. PS4 support arrived in April 2014, opening another way into the rebuilt game. Heavensward followed in 2015, then Stormblood in 2017. Both were major expansions. The game also received regular updates, so the relaunch kept growing beyond its original release. Shadowbringers arrived in 2019. For you, there was more to return to as the years passed. The replacement had become something Square Enix kept developing.

By October 2021, the game had gained over 24 million registered players. Those were registered players. That figure doesn't tell you how many subscriptions were active at the same time. The financial milestone was clearer. By then, the game had become the most profitable Final Fantasy to date. The comparison had expanded. Square Enix could measure the replacement against the rest of its own series. Recovering from the original failure was one achievement; leading the series on profitability was another.

What had Square Enix earned by starting over? We'd call it an earned second launch. Yoshida's team rebuilt while continuing to serve the players the original had disappointed. That gave you something concrete to judge. The company's return to profit showed the rebuilding could support a business, too. The later record established how far that business had grown. The work had consequences beyond getting the servers running again. Square Enix turned a failed release into the most profitable game in Final Fantasy.
